hints: Think about what happens the instant you add extra Q, before the equilibrium has time to respond.
In 1.0 dm3, adding 5.0 mol to 10 mol dm-3 momentarily raises [Q] to 15 mol dm-3, so consider which way Le Chatelier shifts the position.
The shift to the right will use up some but not all of the added Q, so work out where the final [Q] must settle compared to the old and momentary values.
walkthrough:
**Find the concentration just after adding Q**

Think like a teacher watching in slow motion. First you add, then the system reacts.

Initial moles of $Q = 10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \times 1.0 \text{ dm}^{3} = 10 \text{ mol}$

$$\text{new [Q] instant} = \frac{10 + 5.0}{1.0} = 15 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

**Apply Le Chatelier's principle**

Now the system is stressed with too much reactant. It will try to oppose the change.

For the equilibrium:
$$P(aq) + Q(aq) \rightleftharpoons 2R(aq) + S(aq)$$

Increasing $[Q]$ shifts position to the right, so some $P$ and $Q$ react to make more $R$ and $S$.

**Predict the final equilibrium concentration**

The shift uses up some Q, so [Q] must fall back from 15. But it cannot use up all the extra Q, otherwise there would be no reason to shift.

So the new equilibrium $[Q]$ is lower than 15 but still higher than the original 10:
$$10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} < \text{new [Q]}_{eq} < 15 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

options.A: 15 mol dm-3 is only the momentary concentration immediately after dissolving Q. It ignores the shift to the right which then consumes some of the added Q to re-establish equilibrium.
options.B: This is correct. The instant value is 15 mol dm-3, then the position shifts right using up part of the added Q. The final value therefore drops a little from 15 but stays above the original 10 mol dm-3.
options.C: 10 mol dm-3 would mean the system used up all 5.0 mol of added Q to return exactly to the old value. Le Chatelier predicts only a partial opposition, not a complete cancellation, so [Q] must end higher than before.
options.D: A value below 10 mol dm-3 would mean even more Q was consumed than was added. Adding a reactant can never cause its own equilibrium concentration to finish lower than it started, the shift only opposes the increase.
